name: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep
label: Doi Suthep
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/114651040: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wat Phrathat Doi Suthep Racha Worawihan' (365 m across).

text.description: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep is a Theravada Buddhist temple on the mountain of Doi Suthep, about 15 km from Chiang Mai city and 1,073 metres above sea level. Its gold-plated chedi stands 24 metres tall and is the most sacred part of the grounds. It photographs well because you get gold spires, ornate roofs, shrines and statues all within a few steps of each other, and views of the city on the far side of the temple. Tradition says the temple was founded in 1383, when the first stupa was built, and the story of a white elephant carrying a relic up the mountain is told here. Start with the chedi, then step back to include the layered roofs and the pediments, which are the most decorated parts of the buildings. Turn away from the temple for the city view. Inside the halls the light is low, so give your phone a moment to adjust. Remember that this is a working place of worship: dress modestly, take your shoes off where asked, and keep other visitors and worshippers out of the way of your shots.
text.geographic_location: The temple is on the slopes of Doi Suthep, the mountain above Chiang Mai city, about 15 km from the city.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Chiang Mai, the temple can be reached by road; it is about 15 km away. From the car park at the base you can climb the 309 steps beside the Naga balustrade or take the tram up. Once inside, the phone icon on the map is only a few steps from the middle of the complex, less than a minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 10 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the golden chedi and the main buildings. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the courtyard and to fit the tall chedi in from close range. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof details, chofas, Naga figures and the view of the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 10 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the chedi on one of the vertical lines so its spire stays straight. Use a doorway, a shrine roof or a statue in the foreground to add depth. For the city view, face away from the temple and keep some railing or roof edge in the corner to show you are high up.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gold surface to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the gilding keeps its detail instead of turning pale. In the darker halls, tap on a mural, hold the phone steady and let night mode work if it switches on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is usually calmer and gives a clearer view over the city. Late afternoon can give warm light on the gold. Midday is the busiest and the brightest.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship: you must be appropriately dressed and remove your footwear inside the grounds, and ticketing or entry rules may apply, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is usually quieter and often clearer for city views than later in the day.
Late afternoon light can give a warm glow on gold surfaces.
Midday is usually the busiest and brightest time at the temple.
Gold surfaces in strong light can look washed out unless the exposure is lowered slightly.

name: Chiang Mai Night Bazaar
label: Night Bazaar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kalare Night Bazaar' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kalare Night Bazaar' (way/58560283): middle (174 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4307452590: the OpenStreetMap point 'Night Market'.

text.description:
Chiang Mai Night Bazaar is a stretch of market stalls and buildings just east of the old city moat, between the moat and the Ping River. It is known for handicrafts and portrait paintings, with jewellery, toys and clothing alongside. It is described as one of the most popular tourist attractions in Chiang Mai. It began under Chinese merchants, then grew as more commercial buildings went up, and today it has many owners, most of them Thai.

It photographs well after dark, when string lights, neon signs and crowds give you plenty of colour and movement. One visitor guide suggests an elevated walkway beside Kalare Night Bazaar, which looks down on the open-air food court, its stage, the string lights and the people below. Treat it as something to look for nearby rather than a fixed spot. The same guide suggests around 8 PM, when the live band plays and the lights come on.

If you want a second angle, walk to Changklan Road, where a long lane of stalls sits under strung lights and neon signs. Another option is the Iron Bridge, for a quieter riverside view toward the market's night lights; check the angle on the map before you head there. Photography is generally fine, but ask before taking close-ups of stallholders. Keep your phone strap on and a hand free in the crowd.
text.geographic_location: The Night Bazaar is in central Chiang Mai, directly east of the city moat and west of the Ping River. It runs along Chang Khlan Road between Tha Phae Road and Sridonchai Road.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so it is reached on foot from Chang Khlan Road. The bazaar runs along Chang Khlan Road between Tha Phae Road and Sridonchai Road. From the icon, the main stretch is to the north, about 2 minutes on foot. Follow the lit stalls along the road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) to capture the stalls, lights and crowd in one frame, or the food court, stage and crowd if you find the walkway. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the narrow stall lane so the lights overhead fit in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as lanterns or the band on stage.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Kalare Night Bazaar (shoot from the elevated walkway beside the building). An elevated look down onto the open-air food court and its stage, with string lights and the crowd below. Look for it nearby, and check on the day for its exact location.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the busiest part of the scene, such as the stage or food court if you can see it, on one third of the frame, with the string lights across the top. Keep any railing out of the corners. For a different view, try Changklan Road, with the stalls leading away from you under the lights, or the Iron Bridge for a quieter view over the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights keep their colour and do not turn white. Hold the phone steady against a solid surface if there is one. If night mode is on, wait for it to finish, as moving people may blur. Live Photos can capture the band and crowd atmosphere.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around 8 PM, when the live band plays and the string lights are on.

text.access_note: The market streets are open public space, but the food court and any walkway access may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: An elevated walkway beside Kalare Night Bazaar gives a view down onto the food court and stage (from one visitor guide; the stand-here point is not on it).
The live band plays and the string lights come on around 8 PM (from one visitor guide).
Changklan Road is a lane of stalls under strung lights and neon signs, and looks best as the stall lights come on.
The Iron Bridge offers a quieter riverside view toward the market's night lights; check the angle on the day.
Photography is generally allowed, but it is polite to ask before taking close-ups of vendors.
Night mode can blur moving people, and lowering the exposure slider helps keep bright lights from washing out.
The main Night Bazaar stretch is about 2 minutes on foot north of the stand-here point, which is about 150 m south of the subject.

name: Wat Chedi Luang
label: Wat Chedi Luang
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wat Chedi Luang' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/243018795: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wat Chedi Luang' (353 m across).
notes: Ruined giant chedi in the old city.

text.description: Wat Chedi Luang sits in the historic centre of Chiang Mai, and its great brick chedi is the reason to come. Building began in the 14th century and the chedi was finished in the mid-15th century, when it stood about 82 m high with a base some 54 m across, the largest building in all of Lan Na. In 1545 the top 30 m collapsed after an earthquake, which is why it is now a broken, weathered ruin rather than a spire. That worn brick is what makes it photograph so well. After dark, floodlights pick out every crack and ledge, and the east face, where the Emerald Buddha was installed in the niche in 1468, is the best side to photograph. A black jade copy of the Emerald Buddha now sits in the rebuilt eastern niche. The chedi was partly reconstructed in the early 1990s. For phone photos, come after dark or in the first hour after sunrise, when the morning light falls on the eastern face. Keep the whole chedi in the frame, then move in for close shots of the brickwork. If you have time, the carved reliefs of the ho trai (the scripture library) are also worth a look in the morning sun. This is a working temple, so keep your distance from monks and worshippers and avoid photographing them.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Chiang Mai, inside the old city. The temple grounds were once three separate temples, now run together as one.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop serves this spot, so start from the old city centre of Chiang Mai and head to Wat Chedi Luang. The phone icon on the map sits at the subject position within the temple grounds. From there, walk round to the east face of the chedi. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the floodlit chedi after dark. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot fit the whole east face in. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for brick texture and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there you can see the ruined brick chedi lit by floodlights after dark, with its weathered texture clear to see.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the chedi centred and its sides as upright as you can. Include a little foreground, such as the steps or the edge of the niche, to give a sense of scale. For a second picture, take the carved reliefs of the ho trai in morning sun.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest brick to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the floodlit surface does not wash out. After dark, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or your elbows. Use portrait mode only for close detail, not the whole chedi.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, or in the first hour after sunrise.

text.access_note: This is a working Buddhist temple and there may be an entrance charge, so check the official site before you go; dress respectfully and note that photography inside buildings may be restricted.

name: Wat Phra Singh
label: Wat Phra Singh
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wat Phra Singh' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/93414647: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wat Phra Singh' (299 m across).
notes: Most revered temple in the old city.

text.description: Wat Phra Singh is one of the best-known temples in Chiang Mai's Old City, and it rewards a slow wander with a phone in hand. King Phayu of Lan Na founded it in 1345 to hold his father's ashes, and it later became the home of the revered Phra Buddha Sihing image. The compound has several buildings worth framing. The main hall, Viharn Luang, dates from 1924 and is 56 metres long, with a layered Lanna-style teak roof. Viharn Lai Kham, built between 1815 and 1821, is smaller and has gilded decoration. The photo most people come for is the golden bell-shaped chedi (Chedi Than Chang Lom), with elephant reliefs around its base. Gold looks warmest when the sun is low, so late afternoon suits it best, and the white and gold shapes stand out against a blue sky. From the phone icon on the map, aim north at the chedi and let the sky fill the top of the frame. Then walk round for two other exterior shots: the gilded stucco panels on the lower facade of Viharn Lai Kham, and the raised wooden scripture library, Ho Trai, on its stone plinth. Photography inside Viharn Lai Kham is restricted and flash is banned, and Ho Trai is kept locked, so plan on exterior shots only.
text.geographic_location: Wat Phra Singh is in the western part of Chiang Mai's Old City, inside the moat and city walls. The temple compound is large, about 300 metres across.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop serves this part of the Old City, so plan to reach the west side of the Old City, inside the moat, on foot or by local road transport. Once you are at the temple, walk into the grounds to the phone icon on the map at the centre of the compound and aim north at the main chedi. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole chedi. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the elephant reliefs and the gold detail. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only for the long temple roofs or Ho Trai, and keep the phone level so the lines don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the golden bell-shaped Chedi Than Chang Lom with the elephant reliefs at its base, lit by low sun.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the chedi on one side so there is room for sky. Keep the elephants in the lower third. For a second angle, try the gilded panels on the lower facade of Viharn Lai Kham in direct light, or Ho Trai, where the pond beside it may give a reflection (check on arrival).
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gold part of the chedi to set focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the gold keeps its colour and detail instead of going pale. Turn flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, about 4:30 to 5:30 pm, when the low sun warms the gold. Some visitors prefer early morning (about 7:30 to 9:00), which is also worth trying. Songkran in April makes the grounds very crowded.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship; the grounds are otherwise free, but foreign visitors are asked for a small donation to enter Viharn Lai Kham, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Visitors are expected to dress modestly at the temple, with shoulders and knees covered.
Late-afternoon low sun gives the gold a warmer look than midday light.

name: Tha Phae Gate
label: Tha Phae Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tha Phae Square' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Lanna Tha Phae' (pois).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q13016585: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic eastern gate of the old city wall.

text.description: Tha Phae Gate is the eastern gate of Chiang Mai's old walled city and the best known of them all. It is built of red brick in the Lanna style, with a big wooden door in the middle and sections of wall running away on either side. That warm brick against an open square is why it photographs so easily, even in a quick stop. A gate stood here from the time the city was founded in 1296, but what you see today is a reconstruction from the mid-1980s. It is also the only gate of the old inner wall that still has its complete wooden doors. The square in front is a gathering place for festivals such as Yi Peng and Songkran, and the Sunday Walking Street Market starts here. For the classic view, stand in Tha Phae Square and face the gate, with the open plaza and the pigeons in front of it. Early morning is the calmest and best-lit time, when low sunlight rakes across the brick. Crouch a little to bring the pigeons into the foreground. Please do not feed the pigeons, as feeding them may be illegal, and do not lean on or climb the brick walls. On Sunday evenings the market crowds can fill the square, so arrive early if you want a clear frame.
text.geographic_location: Tha Phae Gate is on the eastern side of Chiang Mai's old walled city, with an open square in front of it. The Sunday Walking Street Market starts here and runs along Ratchadamnoen Road.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops are listed near here, so head for the eastern side of Chiang Mai's old walled city and look for the big red-brick gate. From there the gate is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole gate and the plaza in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you crouch low and want the pigeons big in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the brickwork, the roofline and the wooden door.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Tha Phae Square (inside the plaza, facing the gate; one guide says the light is better on the right side when facing the gate). The full red-brick gate with the open plaza and pigeons in the foreground, the classic postcard framing.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the gate in the centre or just above the middle line, with plenty of plaza below. Hold the phone low, near knee height, so the pigeons sit in the foreground. Keep the phone level so the gate's vertical lines don't lean. For a different view after dark, walk to Tha Phae Road, where the lit-up gate stands against the blue sky among warm street lights and traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the brick stays rich. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall for a couple of seconds. Try a Live Photo while the pigeons are moving, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: 6-8 am, when side-light falls on the wall and the square is least crowded. After dark is the time for the gate lit up against a blue sky.

text.access_note: The square and gate are an open public space, but check the official site or local notices before you go in case of festival or market closures.

name: Wat Umong
label: Wat Umong
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wat Umong' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1445519684: the OpenStreetMap point 'Wat Umong (Suan Buddha Dhamma)'.

text.description:
Wat Umong is a wooded temple compound at the foot of Doi Suthep, and it has a tranquil, wooded setting. It is about 700 years old. It was founded by King Mangrai for monks invited from Sri Lanka. Later, King Kue Na restored the stupa and added the walking tunnels the temple is known for. After a long period of abandonment it became a meditation centre in 1949. The grounds cover about 15 acres of trees, paths and a lake.

For photographs, a quiet scene is the wooden platform that reaches out over the lake in the southern part of the compound. From the phone icon on the map you look across still water to trees and a small chedi on the far bank, with everything doubled in the reflection. A guide describes this platform as one of the better quiet photographs in Chiang Mai, and a calmer alternative to the big chedi view. If you have time, the bell-shaped, moss-covered chedi among the trees and the backlit tunnel with a gilded Buddha near the entrance opening both make good second pictures. Keep the platform shot simple: let the water fill the lower half of the frame and leave the trees and chedi as a calm band above it. Wait a moment for people to move out of the picture.
text.geographic_location: Wat Umong is in the western part of Chiang Mai, on Suthep Road at the foot of Doi Suthep. It lies about 1 km south of the main Chiang Mai University campus.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or railway stops nearby, so go by taxi or hired scooter from the Old City. The temple is roughly 4 to 5 km to the west, towards the Doi Suthep hills, so it is not walkable from the centre. Once inside the gate, follow the footpaths to the lake in the southern part of the compound and walk out onto the wooden platform. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the lake, reflection and far bank sit naturally in the frame. If the small chedi looks too distant, step up to the telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to bring the far bank closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the planks of the platform in the foreground, and keep the horizon level.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the trees and the small chedi on the far bank are reflected in the still water in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the water's edge on the lower third line so the reflection is clearly visible. Include a corner of the platform rail if you want some depth, but keep it out of the reflection. If you also want the moss-covered chedi among the trees, or the backlit tunnel view with the gilded Buddha silhouette, treat those as separate pictures from other parts of the grounds.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the far bank to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out and the reflection stays rich. Hold your arms against your body, or rest the phone on the rail, to keep it steady. For the tunnel, tap on the Buddha figure and lower the exposure for a clean silhouette. Don't use flash near Buddha images.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually best, when the water tends to be calmer and the light softer. Avoid windy moments, which ripple the surface and break up the reflection.

text.access_note: This is a working temple and meditation centre. The grounds are generally free, but a small fee for the tunnel is possible, so check on the day, dress modestly, and ask permission before photographing monks or meditators.

name: Wat Chiang Man
label: Wat Chiang Man
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ratchaphakhinai Road' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ratchaphakhinai Road' (way/26765808): middle (44 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/98070869: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wat Chiang Man' (158 m across).
notes: Oldest temple in the city, with elephant-base chedi.

text.description: Wat Chiang Man is a Buddhist temple inside the old city of Chiang Mai. King Mangrai built it in 1297, and it is described as the first temple of the city. The photo here starts at the main gate. Stand on Ratchaphakhinai Road, in front of the gate, and you look into the compound with the main hall and grounds ahead of you. It makes a good opening shot for a set of photos of the visit. Once inside, the Chedi Chang Lom is the picture most people come for. It is the oldest structure in the complex, and the front halves of 15 life-sized brick-and-stucco elephants come out of its second level as if carrying the upper chedi on their backs. A gilded spire sits above them. From a low position the elephants look as though they are walking out of the wall. Parked vehicles on the right of the gate can block the entrance view, so wait for a clear moment. It is a working temple, so stay outside the halls, don't stand on the chedi, and ask before photographing monks or people praying. Check the rules about photography indoors on the day, avoid flash and follow any signs.
text.geographic_location: Wat Chiang Man is inside the walled old city of Chiang Mai. Its main gate faces Ratchaphakhinai Road.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops are listed near this spot. Navigate to Ratchaphakhinai Road and look for the main gate of Wat Chiang Man. From there it is about 3 minutes on foot to the middle of the temple grounds. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the gate view, then switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) inside the courtyard when you are close to the chedi. Use the telephoto lens (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the gilded spire and the elephant details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ratchaphakhinai Road (in front of the main gate, looking into the compound). The temple as you first enter through the main gate, with the main hall and grounds in view. If vehicles are parked on the right side of the gate, wait or come back when the way is clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the gate and the main hall centred, holding the phone level so the buildings don't lean. For a second view, go into the courtyard and get low by the Chedi Chang Lom, so the elephants seem to walk out of the wall with the gilded spire above. The far left corner of the courtyard is another good place, because it shows the full curve of the row of elephants with the spire behind, rather than a flat, straight-on look.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the gilded spire to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the gold keeps its detail. Switch flash off, especially near any hall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the gate area is clear of parked vehicles. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stucco and gold than the middle of the day.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship, so dress modestly and check the official site before you go for any entry or photography rules.

name: Wat Phra That Doi Kham
label: Doi Kham
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wat Phra That Doi Kham' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4463113590: the OpenStreetMap point 'Wat Phra That Doi Kham'.
notes: Hilltop temple with a large white Buddha.

text.description: Wat Phra That Doi Kham sits on a hilltop of about 200 metres in the Mae Hia sub-district of Chiang Mai, and its name means 'Temple of the Golden Mountain's Relic'. The big draw for a phone camera is the 17-metre seated Buddha. Stand in the courtyard in front of it and crouch or hold the phone low: the figure then rises to fill the frame against the sky, with a smaller Buddha and temple roofs and details at the edges. The temple is also known for its very old chedi, said to be around 1,300 years old, and for a sacred relic of the Buddha's hair. Temple records say it was founded in 687 AD. It was left to fall into disrepair for centuries, until the old chedi collapsed after heavy rain in 1966 and a community restoration began. There is also a very tall statue of Thao Wessuwan on site, at 19 metres. If you have time, a second photo is worth taking from Doikham Panorama View Point, which looks over the Chiang Mai plain, the reservoir and the mountains, with the temple's hilltop edge in the foreground. Around sunset the golden chedi catches warm light, and the stairway or Naga-lined steps make a good leading line. Keep out of the way of people praying at the shrines, and note that drones are generally not permitted.
text.geographic_location: Wat Phra That Doi Kham is on top of Doi Kham hill in the Mae Hia sub-district of Chiang Mai. It sits above the city plain, with views towards the city and the mountains.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop nearby; check a map app for the route to Wat Phra That Doi Kham in Mae Hia. The phone icon on the map is in the temple courtyard in front of the big seated Buddha. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) and hold the phone low and tilted up so the 17-metre Buddha fills the frame. If the figure will not fit from where you are standing, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the smaller Buddha and the temple architecture at the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The photo shows the 17-metre seated Buddha filling the frame against a blue sky, with a smaller Buddha and temple architecture at the edges. Crouching low makes the figure look tall.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the Buddha's face on the upper third line, keeping the vertical edges of the base straight. Keep the figure central and let the smaller Buddha and temple details sit at the edges. For a second shot, go to Doikham Panorama View Point for the city plain, the reservoir and the mountains, with the temple's hilltop edge in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the Buddha to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the gold keeps its detail. Don't use portrait mode on the statue, as it can blur the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when shadows and heat are softer. The golden chedi also catches warm light around sunset. Haze in March and April can wash out the city view.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, so dress modestly and keep clear of people praying; entry is described differently in different places (free, by donation or a small fee for the viewpoint), so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Dress modestly (covered shoulders and knees) is the usual expectation at Thai temples.
Early morning light is softer and the golden chedi catches warm light near sunset.
Tilting the phone upwards from a low position makes a tall statue look taller in the frame.
Haze in the March-April burning season can wash out the city view.
Drones are generally not permitted at the site.

name: Warorot Market
label: Warorot Market
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q20558642: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Warorot Market, known locally as Kad Luang, or the "Big Market", is regarded as the largest and best-known market in northern Thailand. It photographs well because everything is close together: piles of dried fruit, northern sausages, chilli pastes, flowers, cloth and embroidery, with shoppers and stallholders moving between them. That gives you plenty of colour and everyday life in one place.

The site was once used for the funeral ceremonies of Chiang Mai's rulers. Princess Dara Rasmi turned it into a market in 1910, and it was named in honour of Prince Intavaroros Suriyavongse, the eighth ruler of Chiang Mai. One part of the market, the alley called Trok Lao Zhou, is linked with Chinese and Hmong traders, so it is a good place to look for handicrafts and local products.

For your phone, think in small scenes rather than one big view. Go for a single stall, a hand reaching for a bag of snacks, or a row of colourful goods. Stay aware of people around you, and ask before you take a close portrait of a stallholder. Keep moving in busy aisles so you don't block the flow. Check the official site or ask locally about the best days and hours before you go.
text.geographic_location: Warorot Market is on Wichayanon Road in Tambon Chang Moi, in Chiang Mai City, close to Chang Khlan Road.
text.directions_text: The market is on Wichayanon Road, close to Chang Khlan Road. Follow the map and head south-east until the stalls begin. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots of stalls and walkways. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in tight alleys to fit in the whole scene. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as food, flowers and fabrics without getting in people's way.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Talat Warorot (second-floor open balcony overlooking the central hall). A top-down view of the ground-floor stalls, vendors and shoppers in the market's central hall. Take a few wider shots on the way, then walk south-east to the market itself and take your close-ups there, stepping to the side of the main aisles.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up an aisle or a row of hanging goods so it leads the eye into the picture. Fill the frame with one colourful stall, and keep a person or a hand in the shot for scale and life. Try portrait mode for plates of food or flowers to blur the busy background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the screen on your subject to focus, then slide the exposure control down a little so bright signs and sunlit gaps don't wash out the colours. Use night mode in dim covered areas, and hold the phone steady against your body or a post. Try a Live Photo to catch movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go earlier in the day, when it is likely to be livelier and the light is softer. Check the official site or ask locally for current opening times.

text.access_note: Warorot Market is a working public market; check the official site before you go for current opening times and any rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Earlier in the day the market is likely to be livelier and the light softer.
Many covered areas inside the market are dim enough to benefit from night mode.
It is polite to ask stallholders before taking close portraits of them.
Narrow alleys and aisles in the market can be crowded, so it helps to step aside when shooting.

name: Wat Suan Dok
label: Wat Suan Dok
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wat Suan Dok' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/322604729: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wat Suan Dok' (342 m across).

text.description: Wat Suan Dok is a large Buddhist temple on the west side of Chiang Mai's old city. Its 48-metre bell-shaped chedi, built in a Sri Lankan style, can be seen from a long way off. The temple was founded in 1370 by King Kue Na of Lanna, on the site of his flower garden, which is where the name "flower garden temple" comes from. The photograph here is the white chedi field in the north-western part of the grounds. This is a cluster of whitewashed memorials that hold the ashes of Chiang Mai's royal family. From the west edge of the field, shooting east, the many small white spires fill the upper part of the frame. The single gilded main chedi is behind you from this spot, so turn around if you want it in a shot. Check where the light falls once you are there. Low sun lights the white chedis from the front and makes them glow, so the late afternoon is the best time to come. If the mountain view is blocked, this angle is a good second choice. A second option is to stand further back in the courtyard and shoot the rows of white chedis with Doi Suthep rising behind them. The wide gable of the main assembly hall, above its twin entrance stairs, also works well. Restoration work has been reported on some chedis near the golden one, so scaffolding may get in the way. Keep your phone steady and shoot with the sun at the side or behind you, to keep the white surfaces clean.
text.geographic_location: Wat Suan Dok is on Suthep Road, on the west side of Chiang Mai's old city moat. It sits roughly one kilometre west of Suan Dok gate, on the way towards Doi Suthep.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stops are listed for this spot. The temple is on Suthep Road, roughly one kilometre west of Suan Dok gate. Once inside the temple grounds, head for the white chedi field in the north-western part of the compound. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole field of white chedis. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out groups of spires. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only for the assembly hall gable when you can't step back far enough.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Shooting east from here, the smaller white chedis are lit from the front by low sun and irregular spire silhouettes fill the top of the frame. The gilded main chedi is behind you from this spot. Check the light on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the rows of white spires along the lower third lines, letting the tips rise into the top of the frame. Crouch slightly so the nearest chedis overlap the ones behind them. If you want the golden chedi, turn around and frame it separately. For a different angle, stand further back in the courtyard and shoot the rows of white chedis with Doi Suthep behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: White walls can fool the exposure. Tap on a white chedi and slide the exposure down a little to keep detail in the stone. If you turn around to shoot the golden chedi, check it in the same way so it does not burn out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around 17:30, when the sun is low. Check where the light falls once you are there, as it depends on the time of year.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship and a university campus, so dress modestly and be discreet inside the buildings. Check the official site before you go for any access or entry rules.

name: Chiang Mai Zoo
label: Chiang Mai Zoo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Huay Kaew Lake' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Art Roastery Huay Kaew' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/105591056: large area 'Chiang Mai Zoo' (1929 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Zoo at the foot of Doi Suthep.

text.description:
Chiang Mai Zoo is a large, hillside zoo of about 200 acres (81 ha) on Huay Kaew Road, just west of Chiang Mai University and at the foot of Doi Suthep. It opened as the official zoo of the province in 1977, after a smaller animal collection first welcomed visitors in 1957. Today it shows around 400 species, from penguins and hippos to tigers and orangutans. It also has a 133-metre aquarium tunnel, opened in 2008 and billed as the world's longest.

From the shore you look across calm water to wooded hills and mountain slopes behind, a green backdrop that suits a scenic zoo shot. Pedal boats are sometimes moored along the edge, which adds a bit of life in the foreground.

The zoo is big and has many different areas, so plan your phone photos around one or two spots instead of trying to cover everything. Keep the lake for wide, relaxed scenes, and use the animal enclosures for close-ups. Check the official site before you go for the latest on entry and what is open.
text.geographic_location: Chiang Mai Zoo lies in the north-west of Chiang Mai, on Huay Kaew Road at the foot of Doi Suthep, just west of Chiang Mai University. Huay Kaew Lake is one of the scenic corners inside the zoo grounds.
text.directions_text: There are no railway or tram stops nearby, so head for Chiang Mai University and continue to the zoo, which is just west of it, by taxi or hired scooter. The middle of the zoo lies about 1.1 km (roughly 1138 m) to the west of the lake; the paths wind, so allow extra time. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lake, hills and sky together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want more of the shoreline. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the wooded hillside or the pedal boats.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Huay Kaew Lake. Calm lake water in the foreground with wooded hills and mountain slopes rising behind it, a green backdrop for zoo scenes. The zoo's central area lies to the west of this spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the water's edge on the lower line, with the hills filling the middle and a little sky on top. Include a patch of shore or a moored boat in the foreground to give the picture depth. Keep the phone level so the lake surface looks flat and calm.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hills to focus, then slide the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. If you get glass reflections at the aquarium or animal windows, hold the phone close to the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water and hills, and the zoo is often quieter early in the day.

text.access_note: The lake is inside the paid zoo grounds, so a zoo ticket is needed; check the official site before you go for entry details and opening times.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on water and hills.
The zoo is often quieter early in the day.
Holding a phone close to glass reduces reflections.
Pedal boats are sometimes moored along the lake shore (from guide notes on the viewpoint).
The paths inside the zoo are winding, so walking between points takes longer than the straight-line distance suggests.

name: Three Kings Monument
label: Three Kings Monument
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1619287904: the OpenStreetMap point 'Three Kings Monument'.
notes: Statues of the founding kings of Lanna.

text.description:
The Three Kings Monument honours Phaya Mangrai, Pho Khun Ramkhamhaeng and Phaya Ngammueang, the three rulers remembered as the founders of the Lanna Kingdom. It stands in the middle of Chiang Mai and marks the founding of the city in 1296. The sculptor was the national artist Kaimook Chuto, who designed and cast it. It was finished in 1983 and opened in 1984, and the figures are about 2.7 metres high.

It photographs well because the three figures make a strong, balanced group, and there is a wide open area in front of it. That space is used for ceremonies, cultural events and community gatherings, so you can step back and fit the whole group in without craning your neck. It also means the scene can look quite different from one day to the next.

That is far enough to show the figures with some of their surroundings, and close enough to bring them in with a little zoom. Keep the three figures together as the main subject, and hold the phone level so the base and the edges of the frame stay straight. If people are standing in front, wait a moment or take a few shots. Then walk closer for a tighter picture of the faces and details.
text.geographic_location: The monument is in the centre of Chiang Mai, on a public open area that is a gathering place for ceremonies and events in the heart of the city.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Chiang Mai and make your way to the monument. Walk westward from there and the statues will be directly ahead of you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene. Switch to telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to bring the three figures closer from where you stand. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk right up to the monument and want to include the open space around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Anusawari Sam Kasat (Three Kings Monument square) (open paving in front of the statues, on the side facing the bronze figures). The three bronze kings on their pedestal, framed by the open square and the trees around it, with the most uncluttered background in the early morning. From here the three figures sit in the middle of the frame with the open public area around them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the group in the centre, with the base near the lower third line. Keep the phone upright and level so the figures do not seem to lean. For a different shot, walk closer and use 2x to fill the frame with the figures alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statues to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the detail of the figures does not turn into a dark silhouette. If you take a Live Photo, hold still for a moment after pressing the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is a good choice, because the sun is then behind you as you face west. Late afternoon puts the sun behind the monument, so check your screen and adjust the exposure.

text.access_note: The open area in front of the monument is a public space used for ceremonies and events, so check the official site before you go if you are planning around a special occasion.

name: Wat Phan Tao
label: Wat Phan Tao
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wat Phan Tao' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/243018378: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wat Phan Tao' (118 m across).
notes: Teak wooden temple next to Wat Chedi Luang.

text.description: Wat Phan Tao is a small, calm temple in the middle of Chiang Mai's old city, right beside Wat Chedi Luang. Its main building is a teak hall that was once a royal residence, which is why it looks different from most temple halls. Above the main door there is a carved peacock decorated with glass, with other Lan Na-style woodcarving around the windows. At the back, a golden bell-shaped chedi is ringed by smaller spires and red-fenced shrines among leafy trees. That is the view the phone icon on the map gives you, and it makes a good alternative to the hall itself. The hall is 21 metres long and 14 metres high, so it is a fair size, but the grounds are fairly compact and easy to walk around. The name means 'temple of a thousand furnaces', a nod to the hearths once used to cast Buddha images. The hall was moved to this spot in 1876. For photos, the gilded chedi works well when the light is low and warm, and the dark teak looks richer then too. Keep some tree branches in the corner of the frame to add depth. Be thoughtful around people who are praying, and avoid pointing your phone at them. There is also a small pond that reflects the hall, plus the entrance carving, so it is worth walking a full circuit before you decide where to shoot.
text.geographic_location: Wat Phan Tao is on Prapokklao Road in the centre of Chiang Mai's old city, in Mueang Chiang Mai district. It sits right next to Wat Chedi Luang.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the old city centre and head for Wat Chedi Luang; Wat Phan Tao is its neighbour, on Prapokklao Road. If you are coming from further out, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Wat Phan Tao. Once you are inside the grounds, walk round behind the hall to the courtyard with the golden chedi, which is the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the chedi and its ring of small spires. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole courtyard, but keep the chedi in the middle so the edges do not stretch it. Use telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out the gilded top and the spires.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand in the courtyard behind the viharn, by the golden chedi. From here you see the gilded chedi surrounded by mini-chedis and red-fenced shrines, among leafy trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the chedi on one of the vertical lines, leaving some leaves at the top or side. Crouch slightly to make the spires look taller. As an alternative, go round to the hall for the teak hall reflected in the small pond, or for the peacock carving above the door.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the golden chedi to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the gold keeps its detail against the sky. For the pond shot, hold the phone still and wait for the water to settle.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, around sunrise or sunset, when the chedi catches warm light. Arrive early during Yi Peng (usually November), as the pond and lantern views get crowded.

text.access_note: This is a working Buddhist temple with free entry to the grounds; dress modestly, look for signs before taking photos inside the hall, and check on-site notices before you go, as the hall has been closed for repairs in the past.
claims_not_in_sources: Dressing modestly is expected at a temple in Thailand.
The gilded chedi catches warm light well at golden hour.
Tree branches in the corner of the frame add depth to the photo.
The pond and lantern views get crowded during Yi Peng, usually in November.

name: Bhubing Palace
label: Bhubing Palace
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Bhubing Palace'.

text.description:
Bhubing Palace is a royal residence on the forested slopes of Doi Buak Ha, above Chiang Mai. It was built in 1961 so the royal family would have somewhere to stay during state visits, and the mountain site was chosen for its cooler air. The building is in the central Thai style known as ruean mu, a group of houses, and it stands on stilts. The royal rooms are upstairs and the entourage's rooms are on the ground floor. Construction took five months, and the first royal guests were King Frederik IX and Queen Ingrid of Denmark in January 1962.

For photographs, the appeal is the mix of calm Thai architecture, tall trees and tidy gardens. The rose gardens (Suan Suwaree) are the most famous part, with temperate plants that are not often grown elsewhere in Thailand. Expect soft green backdrops, flowerbeds that make good foreground colour, and a roofline that looks good against the hillside.

Then wander closer for details such as the stilted base, the roof edges and the flowers. Keep your phone steady, take a few frames of each view, and check the lighting on the screen before moving on. The palace is open to the public except when the royal family is in residence, usually January to March, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Doi Buak Ha, Mueang District, in the hills above Chiang Mai city. It sits on the mountain road that starts at the main entrance of Chiang Mai Zoo.
text.directions_text: No stations or tram stops are listed near the spot. A paved road leads up the hill to the palace from the main entrance of Chiang Mai Zoo. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the palace and its setting. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the rose gardens to take in flowerbeds and building together. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof details and stilts.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front gardens, with the fountain and palace buildings in view). The palace's traditional Thai buildings framed by the front lawns, flower beds and a large fountain.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the palace on one of the third lines, with trees or flowers filling the foreground. Keep the roofline level with the top grid line. In the gardens, hold the phone low and use the flowers as a colourful foreground. Take one wide and one zoomed frame of each view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out the roof. Portrait mode suits close-ups of the roses.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is usually a pleasant time, with cooler air and gentler light, though shade under the trees can be uneven at any hour.

text.access_note: The palace is open to the public except when the royal family is in residence (usually January to March), so check the official site before you go.

name: Wat Chet Yot
label: Wat Chet Yot
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'วัดเจ็ดยอด' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1561708867: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wat Jed Yod' (390 m across).
notes: Seven-spired temple modelled on Bodh Gaya.

text.description: Wat Chet Yot means 'seven-spired temple', and the name describes the photo you come for. The main sanctuary is a rectangular, windowless building with a flat roof. A tall central spire stands on it, with smaller spires around it and two bell-shaped chedis on the side annexes. The design looks to India for its inspiration. King Tilokarat commissioned the temple in 1455 after sending monks to Bagan to study the Mahabodhi Temple, and the building still shows that influence. The grounds are green and spacious, so you can step back far enough to fit the whole building in. The walls carry about 70 stucco reliefs of devas (divine beings), some of them quite weathered. They make good close-up subjects, and they look different from each side, so it is worth walking all the way round the base. The grounds also hold several older Lanna-style chedis, a small ubosot with a carved wooden gable, and a pond with a mondop at the southern end. Photography is allowed, but avoid flash inside the buildings. Take your shoes off before going into the viharn or the inner chamber, and cover your shoulders and knees. Visit when you have time to wander, because the grounds reward a slow loop more than a quick stop.
text.geographic_location: Wat Chet Yot lies north-west of the centre of Chiang Mai, beside the Chiang Mai–Lampang super highway (Highway 11). It sits just north of the crossing of Huai Kaeo Road and Nimmanhemin Road.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are near here. The temple lies north-west of the centre of Chiang Mai, just north of the Huai Kaeo Road and Nimmanhemin Road crossing, beside the super highway. Once inside the grounds, the main chedi is easy to spot and the garden path leads to the front of it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the whole seven-spired chedi and the green grounds into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the stucco figures and the spires.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the central tower up with the middle vertical line, so the spires stand straight. Keep a strip of garden in the foreground to show the green setting. For a second picture, walk closer and use telephoto on the best-preserved devas on the walls with the spires rising above them. Then circle the base, as the carvings look different from each side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the chedi to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Don't use flash inside the buildings. Wipe your lens before you start, because a smudge shows up in bright sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the carvings and fewer harsh shadows. Arrive earlier in the day if you want a quieter garden.

text.access_note: This is a working Buddhist temple, so dress modestly (shoulders and knees covered) and remove your shoes before entering the buildings; opening hours can vary, so check on arrival.

text.description: The Lanna Folklife Museum is a museum in Chiang Mai, devoted to the culture of Northern Thailand. For a phone photographer it is an easy, relaxed stop: the building is the subject, and you can take your time over the frame without a long walk. The building once belonged to the eighth ruler of Chiang Mai, Chao Intavaroros Suriyavongse, and from 1935 it served as the Provincial Courthouse. It was later renovated as a museum, which opened in 2012. Inside, the collections cover Lanna traditions, Buddhist art, ceremonial utensils, and handicrafts such as lacquerware, woven basketry and pottery. Because this is a former courthouse and a former ruler's building, the outside is where a quick photo works best, and the front of the building is the natural place to start. Stand back far enough to get the whole façade in, and keep your phone level so the walls and roofline do not lean. Check the details too: the roof edges, windows and doorways make good closer shots. If you go inside, check the official site before you go to find out what is allowed, as photography rules in museums can vary from room to room.

name: Wat Chedi Liam
label: Wat Chedi Liam
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sheik Istana' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Sheik Istana Hotel' (node/2610440428): point; moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/261636339: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chedi Liam Temple' (163 m across).
notes: Stepped pyramid chedi in the ancient Wiang Kum Kam.

text.description:
Wat Chedi Liam, the "Temple of the Squared Pagoda", is a quiet old temple in the Wiang Kum Kam area. Its tall five-tiered tower is stepped and square-sided, with Buddha figures set into niches and a large lion guarding each corner. The design shows Mon influence from the Haripunchai style and was common in early Lan Na times. The temple was first built around 1287. The buildings you see today come from a renovation in 1908 by a Burmese trader, which is why much of the decoration looks Burmese and most of the Buddha images on the tower wear yellow rather than white. The tower is also the reason the place photographs so well: a strong, simple shape that stands out against the sky.

Separately, one visitor review recommends seeing the stupa from across the Ping River near Sheik Istana, a hotel said to be on the east bank; check this on site. The tower is said to look most striking after dark, when it is lit, with the river in the foreground. For a second angle, walk over to the temple grounds and photograph the full tower with its niches and corner lions, perhaps with a building in front for scale. Keep a respectful distance from monks and anyone praying, and look out for signs about where photography is allowed.
text.geographic_location: Wat Chedi Liam is in the Wiang Kum Kam area of Saraphi district, south-east of central Chiang Mai, off Koh Klang Road. The old walled-city sights are a fair way off, so treat it as a separate trip.
text.directions_text: From central Chiang Mai, head south-east towards the Wiang Kum Kam area by taxi or songthaew. Ask for Wat Chedi Liam. The site is spread out with few amenities, so bring water. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the tower and the sky together, with any river in view. From a distance, try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the tower. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only once you are inside the temple grounds, where you can get close to the tower and keep its full height in the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Sheik Istana (opposite (east) bank of the Ping River, near the hotel). The stupa across the river, most striking at night when it is lit, with the river in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines, with the river, if it is in view, taking the lower third. Keep the phone level so the tower's sides stay straight. For a different angle, go into the temple grounds and photograph the whole tower with a building in front, shot from the east side, or step back to fit in the niches and corner lions.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against a wall or rail to keep the phone still. Tap the lit tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights do not turn white. A Live Photo can also catch movement on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the tower is lit, with the river in the foreground. Dusk is a good alternative, with the sky still holding some colour.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship in a spread-out site: dress modestly and respect monks, and check the official site or local signs before you go about access and where photography is allowed.
claims_not_in_sources: The stupa is best seen from across the Ping River, especially at night when it is lit (from a visitor review of the area near Sheik Istana).
Sheik Istana is on the east bank of the Ping River (from one review; needs verifying on site).
Wat Chedi Liam is reached by taxi or songthaew from central Chiang Mai.
Dressing modestly is expected at a working temple.
Photography may be restricted inside some buildings, and the chedi itself is reported to be off-limits to women.
The site has few amenities.

label: Wat Mengrai
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'วัดพระเจ้าเม็งราย' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'วัดพระเจ้าเม็งราย' (way/691917810): middle (124 m across).

notes: Old city temple dedicated to King Mengrai.

text.description:
Wat Phra Chao Mengrai is a small Buddhist temple in the old city of Chiang Mai, founded at the start of the 14th century by King Mangrai, the first king of Lan Na and the founder of Chiang Mai. It was once called Wat Kalakot or Wat Khan Kad, and took its present name in the 1950s. One story says the king chose the site after a cart carrying a Buddha image broke down here, and he took that as an omen to build a temple on the spot.

For a phone photo, the most obvious picture is the ornate ceremonial gate and archway at the main entrance, with the temple buildings visible behind it. Inside, the Lanna-style main viharn has a tiered roof, naga bargeboards and decorated gable ends. There is also a square chedi with a niche for a Buddha image on each of its four sides. The temple is known for a bronze walking Buddha image, over five metres tall, dating from the early 14th century. It stands in its own sala, so look for it as you wander.

The temple is quiet and not heavily visited, so you should have time to try a few angles without waiting. Start with the gate from the street, then move inside for the viharn roofline and the chedi. Please be discreet around anyone praying, and keep your phone low and quiet near the Buddha images.
text.geographic_location: Wat Phra Chao Mengrai is in the old city of Chiang Mai, a quiet temple.
text.directions_text: This point is about 249 m east of the temple's mapped position, so walk west from it to reach the temple. You can search the map for the Thai name, วัดพระเจ้าเม็งราย. Street addresses for this temple vary between listings, so trust the temple's location on the map rather than a written address. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the gate, as it shows the archway and the buildings behind it without distortion. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the street is too narrow to fit the whole gate. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the roof finials, gable ends and the gilt top of the chedi.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (main entrance gate, framed from the street). The temple's ornate ceremonial gate and archway with the compound's buildings visible behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the archway and turn on gridlines so the gate posts stay upright. Keep a little of the buildings behind it in view to give a sense of the temple. Once inside, a second picture is the Lanna-style main viharn, with its tiered roof, naga bargeboards, chofa finials and decorated gable ends. A third is the square chedi, with its standing Buddha images in niches and the gilt finial above the bell-shaped top.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gate to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out the gold detail. Take a few shots with the zoom at different levels, as the detail on the roofs and finials is worth picking out. Use Live Photos only if you want a moving moment, such as someone walking through the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No best time of day is given for this temple. Gentle morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder on gilded detail than harsh midday sun. Opening hours may vary, so check on the day.

text.access_note: This temple is free to enter and open-air, but opening hours may vary, so check on the day.
